title: The Ajanta copies that burned twice
seo_title: The Ajanta copies that burned twice: Robert Gill, John Griffiths and the fires of 1866 and 1885
meta_description: Two teams spent decades copying the Ajanta murals in oil. Fire destroyed most of Robert Gill's canvases in 1866 and over a hundred of John Griffiths's in 1885. What survives, and why it matters.
og_title: The Ajanta copies that burned twice
og_description: Nineteen years of painting in a cave, lost in one night at the Crystal Palace. Then it happened again.
summary: The murals of Ajanta, dated by the V&A from the 1st century BCE to about 480 CE, were already deteriorating when the British began copying them. Robert Gill, an army officer, painted about thirty large oil copies between 1844 and 1863; most were destroyed when fire swept the Crystal Palace at Sydenham in December 1866, and four survive at the V&A. From 1872 John Griffiths and seven students of the Bombay School of Art made about 300 more; in June 1885 another fire in a London store destroyed, by the V&A's account, well over a hundred of them. What survived, with Griffiths's printed plates of 1896–97, is now evidence of what the walls once showed.

paras: At about two o'clock on Sunday 30 December 1866, fire broke out at the Crystal Palace at Sydenham, south London, and burned down its north transept. The Spectator, reporting the following Saturday, put it down to what seemed an explosion of gas. By the time it was out, the tropical section had gone and the Indian Court, among others, was described as 'irreparably injured'.

The Indian Court held a set of paintings that no one else in the world could have made again. They were full-size oil copies of the murals in the Buddhist caves at Ajanta, in today's Maharashtra, painted on the spot by one army officer over more than a decade. Most of them burned that afternoon.

The thirty or so caves of Ajanta are cut into a horseshoe bend of rock above the Waghora river. Their walls and ceilings carry some of the earliest surviving mural painting in India: the V&A dates it from the 1st century BCE to about 480 CE. After the caves were abandoned, the jungle took them back. A British army officer out hunting came upon them in 1819, and once exposed, the paintings began to deteriorate.
If the murals were to be studied anywhere but in the caves, someone had to copy them.

In 1844, by the V&A's account, an army officer, Robert Gill, was commissioned to copy them. His copying ran until 1863. Working in oils and at full size, he produced about thirty large canvases of the principal paintings. Buckland's Dictionary of Indian Biography (1906) calls him 'antiquary, artist and sportsman', and credits him with killing more than 150 tigers.

Gill also took up the camera. Seventy-four of his photographs illustrated James Fergusson's The Rock-Cut Temples of India, published by John Murray in London in 1864. The canvases, meanwhile, were sent to England. Those on display at Sydenham were lost in 1866. Four of Gill's copies survive at the Victoria and Albert Museum; one, dated 1856, shows a painting from Cave 1.

The loss was not accepted. From 1872, John Griffiths (1837–1918) of the Bombay School of Art spent every winter at the caves with seven Indian students of the school. They kept at it for thirteen years and produced about 300 paintings. On several canvases, on the edges turned over the stretcher, the painters wrote in red paint the dates they began and finished; one large copy took about five months of work, by the V&A's reckoning. At least one canvas carries the pencilled name of a student, Pestonji Bomanjie.
The V&A puts the cost of the project at £30,000. The finished copies were sent to London.

Then it happened again. In June 1885 a fire broke out in a London storeroom where the copies were kept and, by the V&A's own account, destroyed well over a hundred canvases. Scorched survivors are still in the collection: the V&A's record for a copy of a strip of floral decoration from Cave 6 notes that it 'has been badly damaged by fire'.

Griffiths had one thing Gill had not: print. His selection of the copies was published as The Paintings in the Buddhist Cave-Temples of Ajantâ, Khandesh, India, in two large volumes, by order of the Secretary of State for India (London: W. Griggs, 1896 and 1897). The first volume covers the pictorial subjects, the second the decorative details. Those plates outlived the canvases that burned.

sections.h2: What survives, and why copies count as evidence
paras: In 2006 the V&A's curator and conservator counted 166 copies of the Ajanta paintings in the museum, from half a metre square to three metres by six, made between 1844 and 1885 in the campaigns of Gill and Griffiths. In 2005 the museum cleaned 81 of them and moved them to better storage.

A copy is not the original. It carries the copyist's eye and the conventions of a Victorian art school. But it records a wall as it looked on the day it was painted, and the walls at Ajanta have gone on changing since. When a detail has flaked away in the cave, a dated copy, or a photograph by Gill, can be the only record of what was there. That is why a copy is read like any other historical document, asking each time who made it, when, and how faithfully.

A third campaign followed. Christiana Herringham and her assistants copied some of the paintings in 1909–1911, published in 1915 by Oxford University Press as Ajanta Frescoes, with essays by members of the India Society.

Griffiths's two volumes and Lady Herringham's Ajanta Frescoes are long out of copyright, and libraries have digitised them: the Smithsonian Libraries' scan of Ajanta Frescoes is free to read online. Set a plate beside a recent photograph of the same wall and you will see, scene by scene, what has been lost. Read the dates as well as the pictures: a copy finished in the 1870s shows the wall as it stood in the 1870s, not as it was painted. The V&A's surviving copies are in store and can be seen by appointment through its collections website.
At Ajanta itself, the caves are an Archaeological Survey of India site in Maharashtra and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

sections.h2: Learn to read what you are looking at
paras: A mural, a relief or a copy of either is read the same way: by its gestures, its costume, its setting and the conventions of its makers. Talaash Heritage's [Identifying sculpture](reading-sculpture.html) programme teaches exactly that, and our guides to [Buddhist caves in India](buddhist-caves-in-india.html) and [heritage sites in Maharashtra](heritage-sites-in-maharashtra.html) take you further. Next Sunday, 6 December, Durlabh #03 is 'Read Brāhmī, a first lesson'.

faq.q: Who copied the Ajanta paintings in the 19th century?
faq.a: Robert Gill, from 1844 to 1863 by the V&A's account, and then John Griffiths with seven students of the Bombay School of Art, every winter from 1872 to 1885. Lady Herringham's team copied some paintings again in 1909–1911.

faq.q: What happened to Robert Gill's copies?
faq.a: He painted about thirty. Most were destroyed in the fire at the Crystal Palace, Sydenham, in December 1866. Four survive at the Victoria and Albert Museum, London.

faq.q: How many of Griffiths's copies were lost?
faq.a: His team made about 300. A fire in a London storeroom in June 1885 destroyed well over a hundred, according to the V&A, which counted 166 surviving copies from the two campaigns in 2006.
The V&A's copies are in store and viewable by appointment. Griffiths's printed volumes (1896–97) and Herringham's Ajanta Frescoes (1915) are digitised by several libraries.
